prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: They, The, Saying

outputs.L1:
They sent him back to her. The letter came, saying that she could have him. Before she could be certain there was no hidden ill beneath the formal words, he was there—alive. They had given him back to her alive. How else? They were not known to send back the dead. Nor was he visibly disfigured. His face? His hands? She had to look and ask, “What was it, dear?”

She had given everything, and still she had everything. They had everything—they were the fortunate ones. Was she not glad now? Everything seemed won, and all that remained to them was the permissible ease of relief.

Still, she had to ask, “What was it, dear?”

“Enough, yet not enough. A bullet passed clean through, high in the breast. Nothing that good care, medicine, rest, and a week with you cannot cure—so that I may go again.”

The same grim sacrifice was to be endured once more by them both. She dared ask only with her eyes how he felt about facing a second trial. With his eyes, he asked her not to ask.

They had given him back to her—but not to keep.
outputs.L2:
They returned him to her. First came the official letter saying that he was hers again. Before she could convince herself that its stiff, formal language concealed no terrible news, he arrived in person—alive. Of course he was alive; they did not send home the dead. Nor did he appear outwardly mutilated. She searched his face and hands, then asked, “What happened, darling?”

She had surrendered everything, yet now it seemed she had lost nothing. They still possessed one another—how fortunate they were. Surely she could feel happy now. It appeared that they had triumphed, with only comfort and rest ahead of them.

Still, she needed to know. “What happened, darling?”

“It was serious, though not serious enough. A bullet passed straight through the upper part of my chest. But with proper treatment, medicine, rest, and a week with you, I’ll recover—and then I can return.”

Once again, both of them faced the same harsh sacrifice. She could only question him silently, wondering whether he could endure being sent back a second time. His answering look begged her not to say it aloud. He had been restored to her, but only temporarily.
outputs.L3:
The soldier was returned to her alive, and for one fleeting moment, relief eclipsed everything else. She held him close, scarcely able to believe that he had survived the battle and found his way back to her. Then anxiety took over. She searched his face and body for signs of injury until she learned that a bullet had passed through his upper chest. The wound was serious, but it had spared his life.

He tried to reassure her. With proper medical care, enough rest, and a week spent by her side, he believed he would regain his strength and be ready to return to the war. He spoke as though recovery were a simple matter of time, but neither of them could ignore what his recovery would mean.

In the silence between them, they shared the same unspoken dread. Soon, they might be forced to endure another separation, another long period of uncertainty, and the possibility that next time he might not come back. She was deeply grateful that he had been restored to her alive, yet her relief was shadowed by a painful truth: he had been returned to her only briefly, not permanently.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents the return of a wounded soldier primarily through his wife’s anxious perspective. Rather than treating his homecoming as a moment of uncomplicated relief, it emphasizes her uncertainty as she waits to discover the extent of his injuries and what they will mean for their future. Her fear shapes the scene, making even ordinary gestures and words feel tense. The restrained dialogue between husband and wife deepens this effect: neither openly expresses the full weight of their emotions, yet their pauses and careful exchanges suggest shock, vulnerability, and the difficulty of speaking honestly about physical suffering and possible loss.

When the couple finally confronts the soldier’s wound, his survival offers only limited comfort. He has returned alive, but he has not truly escaped the war. His injury has entered their home and altered the emotional life they share. Moreover, the expectation that he will recover and be sent back to fight transforms the reunion into a temporary reprieve rather than a lasting homecoming. The poem therefore resists any simple celebration of survival. Instead, it reveals how war continues to exert pressure on soldiers and their families even when the immediate danger has passed. Through the wife’s fear, the husband’s wounded body, and the couple’s subdued conversation, the poem exposes the relentless emotional toll of a conflict that repeatedly separates them and denies them any secure sense of peace.
outputs.L5:
**What They Were Saying**

They gathered beneath the old oak tree, where the evening wind carried every whisper farther than intended. The truth had been hidden for years, buried beneath polite smiles and unfinished conversations.

No one remembered who began saying it aloud. Perhaps it was the baker, the teacher, or the child who listened too carefully. But soon, the secret traveled from door to door.

“They knew,” people murmured.

The words changed with every telling, yet their meaning remained. By morning, the whole town understood: silence could protect a secret, but it could never erase the truth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite Robert Frost’s poem “Not to Keep.”
counterfactuals.output:
**“Not to Keep” — Robert Frost**

They sent him back to her. The letter came  
Saying . . . and she could have him. And before  
She could be sure there was no hidden ill  
Under the formal writing, he was in her sight—  
Living.—They gave him back to her alive—  
How else? They are not known to send the dead—  
And not disfigured visibly. His face?—  
His hands? She had to look—to ask,  
“What was it, dear?” And she had given all  
And still she had all—they had—they the lucky!  
Wasn’t she glad now? Everything seemed won,  
And all the rest for them permissible ease.  
She had to ask, “What was it, dear?”  
“Enough,  
Yet not enough. A bullet through and through,  
High in the breast. Nothing but what good care  
And medicine and rest—and you a week,  
Can cure me of to go again.” The same  
Grim giving to do over for them both.  
She dared no more than ask him with her eyes  
How was it with him for a second trial.  
And with his eyes he asked her not to ask.  
They had given him back to her, but not to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
